The only crittical portion of installation is the disk stuff. All other installation defaults can't cause trouble so pay attention to just this one.

Do not select replace my operating system, obviously. Select "do something else instead". But lets rewind a bit to make this step easier.

Boot the disk into "try ubuntu without installing" mode. This lets you sample ubuntu.. without installing obviously. But lets us also use programs. Open up gparted from the start menu. Shrink down your ntfs partition and place in an ext4 and a swap (swap at 2 gig). These are file system formats. The ext4 is going to be getting the linux.

Now go to the desktop and click install ubuntu. Now when we get to the "do something else" your disk is pre-prepped. You can see each partition and can "edit" them. The thing to "edit" is the mount point. Select "/" for the ext4. That's the unix equivelent to C:\.

Now continue with the rest of the installation and every default is fine.

This only really presents when you have an external monitor connected, and you're using your laptop as a second monitor; the laptop's monitor tries to run off of the Intel card, while the external runs off of the NVidia, causing a sync issue and a permanent panning setting on the external that can only be overridden with an xrandr hack that totally fubars your 3D rendering. But this is an NVidia bug, and not related to any particular desktop environment; also, you can work around this by using just one monitor while gaming.

TL;DR: you might run into some issues, but Google and the CLI are your friends. Good luck!

Beware of Secure Boot. If Linux refuses to boot, secure boot might be the problem. You can disable it in the UEFI menu (often incorrectly referred to as the BIOS -- UEFI replaces the BIOS). Depending on your distro, you might also have to turn on Legacy boot mode (which emulates a BIOS, and can boot older OSes that don't have UEFI support). Distro hop around!

Ubuntu is just fine--I'm not bashing on it--but try multiple distros. For newbies, I'd try out any spin of Ubuntu, Fedora (my fav), Debian, OpenSuse (weird installer), or SolusOS (new). Using a different distro is a big eye-opener to what different distros do and what your own preferences are.

After a bit of normal use, set up a virtual machine or tiny partition to try something that really pushes your limits--whether it's a distro like Arch or a project like switching the filesystem to ZFS and using a RAID array.

Lurk around on /v/unixpix, /v/linux, /v/linuxmasterrace, /v/linuxgaming, /v/[your-distro], /v/[some-other-distro], etc. You'll pick up half your knowledge there.

Take risks. See how long it takes for you to break your computer. My record is 5 minutes; see if you can do it faster than that. Fixing problems is where you'll pick up the other half of your knowledge.
